section.title: The Servant of the Lord
section.sectionRationale: This chapter contains the first of Isaiah's Servant Songs, verses 1 to 9, one of the Book of Comfort's most important passages, introducing a gentle, Spirit-filled Servant who will bring justice to the nations without breaking a bruised reed. The chapter then turns to contrast this ideal Servant with Israel's own blindness and deafness, showing the gap between the calling and the nation's actual failure to keep it.
section.thesis: The LORD presents His chosen Servant, gentle enough not to break a bruised reed yet faithful enough to establish justice on the earth, as a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, and then exposes that Israel itself, called to this very role, has been blind and deaf, unable to fulfill the calling only the true Servant can complete.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the first Servant Song introducing the gentle, justice-bringing Servant; His mission as covenant and light to the nations; a new song of praise summoned from all the earth; the LORD roused to act like a warrior and a woman in labor; the searching question of who is blind but God's own servant; and the closing lament over a plundered, uncomprehending people.

verses.text: “Here is My {{ebed|Servant}}, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will bring {{mishpat|justice}} to the nations.
He will not cry out or raise His voice, nor make His voice heard in the streets.
A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice.
He will not grow weak or discouraged before He has established justice on the earth. In His law the islands will put their hope.”

units.label: A covenant for the people, a light to the nations

verses.text: This is what God the LORD says, He who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and its offspring, who gives breath to the people on it and life to those who walk in it:
“I, the LORD, have called you for a righteous purpose, and I will take hold of your hand. I will keep you and appoint you to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations,
to open the eyes of the blind, to bring prisoners out of the dungeon and those sitting in darkness out from the prison house.
I am the LORD; that is My name! I will not yield My glory to another or My praise to idols.
Behold, the former things have happened, and now I declare new things. Before they spring forth I proclaim them to you.”

units.label: Sing to the LORD a new song
units.note: praise from the ends of the earth

verses.text: Sing to the LORD a new song, His praise from the ends of the earth, you who go down to the sea, and all that is in it, you islands, and all who dwell in them.
Let the desert and its cities raise their voices; let the villages of Kedar cry aloud. Let the people of Sela sing for joy; let them cry out from the mountaintops.
Let them give glory to the LORD and declare His praise in the islands.
The LORD goes forth like a mighty one; He stirs up His zeal like a warrior. He shouts; yes, He roars in triumph over His enemies:

units.label: I will groan like a woman in labor

verses.text: “I have kept silent from ages past; I have remained quiet and restrained. But now I will groan like a woman in labor; I will at once gasp and pant.
I will lay waste the mountains and hills and dry up all their vegetation. I will turn the rivers into dry land and drain the marshes.

I will lead the blind by a way they did not know; I will guide them on unfamiliar paths. I will turn darkness into light before them and rough places into level ground. These things I will do for them, and I will not forsake them.
But those who trust in idols and say to molten images, ‘You are our gods!’ will be turned back in utter shame.

units.label: Who is blind but My servant?

verses.text: Listen, you deaf ones; look, you blind ones, that you may see!
Who is blind but My servant, or deaf like the messenger I am sending? Who is blind like My covenant partner, or blind like the servant of the LORD?
Though seeing many things, you do not keep watch. Though your ears are open, you do not hear.”
The LORD was pleased, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify His law and make it glorious.
But this is a people plundered and looted, all trapped in caves or imprisoned in dungeons. They have become plunder with no one to rescue them, and loot with no one to say, “Send them back!”
Who among you will pay attention to this? Who will listen and obey hereafter?
Who gave Jacob up for spoil, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned? They were unwilling to walk in His ways, and they would not obey His law.
So He poured out on them His furious anger and the fierceness of battle. It enveloped them in flames, but they did not understand; it consumed them, but they did not take it to heart.

ebed.gloss: Servant, one who serves under another's authority, sometimes with great honor, as of Moses or David. Here it introduces the first of Isaiah's Servant Songs, a figure the LORD upholds and delights in, whom the New Testament directly identifies as Jesus, the Servant who succeeds where the nation Israel, also called God's servant elsewhere in these chapters, repeatedly failed.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the right ordering of relationships and society according to God's own character. The Servant's mission, repeated three times in the opening verses, is to bring, establish, and faithfully deliver this justice to the nations, not through force or noise but through patient, gentle faithfulness that will not break even a bruised reed.

basic.context: This chapter opens with one of Isaiah's most treasured passages, the first Servant Song, introducing a figure the LORD upholds, delights in, and fills with His Spirit to bring justice to the nations, gently, without crushing the weak or extinguishing the faltering. The chapter then turns painfully honest: the very nation called to be God's servant and light to the world is itself blind and deaf, plundered because of its own disobedience.
basic.hermeneutics: Isaiah elsewhere calls the nation Israel God's servant, but this Servant is presented with a mission to Israel itself, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners, suggesting a figure distinct from and greater than the nation, someone who succeeds where Israel failed. The New Testament resolves the question directly: Matthew 12:15-21 quotes this very passage and applies it explicitly to Jesus.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter's central figure is the {{ebed}}, the Servant, upheld and chosen by God, whose mission is to bring {{mishpat}}, justice, to the nations, a word repeated three times in the opening verses alone. The chapter's tragic turn shows Israel itself failing to embody either the Servant's justice or its own calling as God's covenant partner, blind and deaf despite having eyes and ears.
basic.typology: The gentle Servant who will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick anticipates Jesus' whole pattern of ministry, healing the broken and encouraging the faltering rather than crushing them. Israel's failure as a blind, deaf servant sets up the need for a Servant who succeeds fully where the nation could not, fulfilled in Christ, the true Israel who keeps the covenant perfectly.
basic.christ: Matthew 12:15-21 quotes this passage in full and applies it directly to Jesus, whose quiet, healing ministry, avoiding public spectacle while gently restoring the broken, is presented as the very fulfillment of the Servant Song. Jesus is the covenant for the people and light to the nations, verse 6, echoed in Luke 2:32 and Acts 13:47, opening blind eyes both physically and spiritually, verse 7, exactly as He does throughout the Gospels.
basic.god: God delights in His Servant and entrusts Him with a mission of justice carried out through gentleness rather than force, refusing to share His glory with any idol. He is also painfully honest about His own people's failure, naming their blindness and deafness plainly rather than excusing it, while still working through the ideal Servant to accomplish what Israel could not.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 12:15-21 quotes Isaiah 42:1-4 directly and applies it to Jesus' ministry. Luke 2:32 calls Jesus 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles,' echoing verse 6. Acts 13:47 applies the same 'light to the nations' language to the apostolic mission. John 8:12 has Jesus declare Himself the light of the world.
basic.oneStory: This chapter introduces the Servant who will succeed at exactly the mission Israel, God's other servant, failed to fulfill: bringing justice and light to the nations gently and faithfully. That Servant is revealed in the New Testament to be Jesus, who fulfills this song word for word, opening blind eyes and refusing to crush the weak, accomplishing what neither Israel nor any human effort could achieve.

context.literary:
Isaiah 42 is built as a hinge. Its first nine verses are a legal presentation: God speaks about someone in the third person in verses 1 to 4, then turns and speaks to him in the second person in verses 5 to 9. The word 'Behold' that opens verse 1 is the same word that opened the great summons of Isaiah 40:9 and 40:10, and it is set against the rival gods of Isaiah 41:24 and 41:29, which the same chapter calls empty. Here at last is the one who is real.

Verses 10 to 17 are a hymn that breaks out at the end of the oracle, the first of several in the Book of Comfort, and its mood swings from song to battle. The 'new song' is answered at once by the warrior of verse 13 and the labouring woman of verse 14, so praise and violence sit side by side. Verses 18 to 25 turn the whole chapter around. The same vocabulary that described the Servant's work, eyes that open, prisoners brought out, is now applied to the nation. The one sent to open blind eyes is mirrored by a servant whose own eyes are shut.

Two rhetorical devices hold this together. First, a quiet wordplay joins verses 3 and 4: the reed that is 'bruised' and the wick that is 'smoldering' are named in verse 3, and in verse 4 the Servant himself 'will not grow weak,' with the same Hebrew roots, so that what He refuses to do to the weak He refuses to undergo Himself. Second, verses 19 to 20 pile up four questions in a row, 'Who is blind but My servant?', in a staccato that reads like an accusation in court. The chapter ends with a sentence that has no resolution: they were burned and 'did not take it to heart,' verse 25, and the next chapter must answer.
context.historical:
The first hearers were the exiles of the sixth century, or the people of Judah being prepared for them. Their world was an empire of heavy hands. Babylon's kings boasted of their strength and their gods, and subject peoples learned that justice belonged to whoever held the sword. Into that world the oracle sets a ruler who does not shout in the street, verse 2. In the ancient Near East a king's rule was announced in proclamations and parades; a ruler who works without volume would have sounded like no ruler at all.

The geography of verse 11 is quietly pointed. Kedar was an Arabian tribe of the northern desert, and Sela is usually taken as a rock city in Edom, though the identification is uncertain. These were peoples who lived at the edges of Israel's map, and they are called to sing. The 'islands' or coastlands of verses 4, 10 and 12 were the farthest horizon to a people whose sea was the Mediterranean. The Servant's reach is meant to run to the places where Israel had never carried its law.

Verses 22 to 25 look back on what the exiles knew first hand: villages stripped, people hidden in caves and held in pits, with no one to demand their return. 'Send them back' is the language of redemption or restitution, the cry of a kinsman, and the verse says plainly that no one spoke it. The prophet then names the reason that Israel's own history already gave, the long record of breaking the covenant that Moses had warned would end in just this fire, Deuteronomy 28:49-52 and 32:22.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 42:1-4 is the first of the four passages scholars call the Servant Songs, and each one deepens the portrait. Isaiah 49:1-6 hears the Servant describe His own calling and His discouragement, and there the task is enlarged: it is 'not enough' to restore Israel, for He is also to be a light to the nations, 49:6. Isaiah 50:4-9 gives Him the ear of a disciple and a face set like flint under blows. Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12 brings Him to death and out of it. The gentleness of chapter 42 is the opening note of a song that ends at a grave, and the later songs show the cost of the refusal to break the bruised.

The Spirit resting on the Servant, 42:1, joins a thread that runs from the shoot of Jesse, Isaiah 11:2, to the anointed preacher of Isaiah 61:1. The Servant's task of bringing prisoners out of the dungeon, 42:7, is picked up in 49:9 and 61:1. In the New Testament Matthew 12:15-21 quotes the whole of verses 1 to 4, in a rendering that departs from both the Hebrew and the Greek in places and ends with 'the nations will put their hope in His name,' where the BSB footnote on Isaiah 42:4 records that the Septuagint reads 'name.' At His baptism the voice from heaven joins words from the royal Psalm 2:7 and, most readers hold, from this verse, Matthew 3:17. Paul uses the 'light to the nations' of verse 6 to explain his own mission, Acts 13:47, and Simeon uses it of the baby in his arms, Luke 2:32.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet is not mainly writing a character sketch. He is settling a dispute about who can be trusted to do what Israel could not. The exiles had a settled belief about justice: it is imposed by force, and their God, who had let Jerusalem burn, appeared to have none. Verses 1 to 9 answer by describing a different kind of power, patient, quiet, and sure to finish, and verse 4 insists on that last point with two negatives, 'He will not grow weak or discouraged.' Israel is meant to take heart that the work does not depend on the exiles' strength.

Verses 18 to 25 make the second move, and it is the harder one. The prophet wants the nation to recognise itself in the blind servant, so that the portrait of the ideal Servant does not become a comfortable story about someone else. The sequence matters: He offers the Servant first, then holds up the mirror. The hearers are meant to feel both the relief of a rescuer and the weight of their own deafness, so that they will turn and listen to the one voice that has been speaking since Isaiah 40:1.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first nine verses describe a particular person and a particular mission, and they are not given as a pattern the reader is simply to copy. Believers are not appointed to be the covenant and the light in the way the Servant is, though the New Testament does draw them into the work, as Paul does with Acts 13:47 and Jesus does when He sends Paul to open eyes, Acts 26:18. The honest reading is that we share in His mission because we are united to Him, and not because verse 6 has been handed on to us directly.

What does carry across is the manner. The description of a ministry that does not break the bruised reed is a standing rebuke to leadership that wins by shouting or by wounding, and the same goes for the church's pastoral work. Verses 18 to 25 are a different kind of text: a diagnosis of a historical judgment, not a rule of thumb that every disaster is God's discipline for a specific sin. The prophet names Israel's sin here because he is speaking with prophetic authority about this exile; the book of Job warns against drawing that line for others.

debates.question: Who is the blind servant of verse 19, and how does he relate to the Servant of verse 1?

views.label: Two different servants
views.case: The Servant of verses 1 to 9 is faithful and successful, while the servant of verses 18 to 20 is blind and deaf. The Servant of the first part opens blind eyes, verse 7, so the second servant must be the people He has come to help. The two are therefore distinct: Israel in her failure, and the Servant who rescues her. Isaiah 41:8 and 44:1 name the nation 'My servant' just as plainly.

views.label: One servant seen from two sides
views.case: Others hold that Israel is one servant with an ideal and a reality, and that the prophet moves from what the servant is called to be to what it has become. On this reading the Servant of verse 1 is the faithful remnant or even the ideal Israel, and the second half simply names the gap. The Septuagint's addition of 'Jacob' and 'Israel' to verse 1 shows that some early readers heard the nation in the first part too.

debates.bearing: The two views need not be opposed in the end. The text holds the tension on purpose, and the later songs resolve it: in 49:3 the Servant is called 'Israel,' yet in 49:5 He is sent to bring Israel back to God. The Servant stands in Israel's place, doing what Israel was meant to do, and the New Testament reads Jesus as the one in whom the calling is finally kept.

debates.question: What do 'justice' and 'His law' mean in verses 1 to 4, and is there a sword behind the gentleness?

views.label: Justice as a restored social order
views.case: The word is used of right ordering in society, protecting the weak and settling cases fairly, and the gentle Servant is the true king who does this without force, in the manner of Isaiah 11:3 and 11:4. His 'law' is the teaching that the islands wait for, and the nations come to Him as to a teacher.

views.label: Justice as victory over evil as well as care for the weak
views.case: Verse 13 pictures the LORD as a warrior who roars in triumph over His enemies, and verse 15 lays waste the landscape. Justice here includes judgment, and the gentleness of verses 2 and 3 is aimed at the weak, not at the oppressor. Matthew's 'till He leads justice to victory' keeps the note of conquest.

debates.bearing: Both are in the text, and they are not in competition. The Servant refuses to crush the weak while He sets Himself against the powers that crush them. The New Testament places the gentle ministry and the final reckoning at different times, but under one Lord, Matthew 12:20 and Revelation 19:11-16.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 names two images of weakness, and each has a precise Hebrew shape. The 'bruised reed' is a qaneh ratsuts, from a root that means to crush or break, the same root that later describes Egypt as a 'broken reed,' Isaiah 36:6. The 'smoldering wick' is a pishtah kehah, where kehah means dim or faint, the same family that describes failing eyes in Genesis 27:1 and Deuteronomy 34:7. Verse 4 then says the Servant will not 'grow weak' and will not be 'discouraged,' and these are the verbs yikheh and yaruts, built on those very roots. A reader who knows the Hebrew hears the Servant promise Himself that He will not be what He refuses to make others, dimmed and crushed.

The verb 'I uphold,' verse 1, is tamakh, to grasp or hold fast, and the Servant is called a 'Chosen One,' bachir. Verse 1 says 'My soul delights' in Him, from ratsah, the verb of acceptance and favour that describes a sacrifice that is accepted, Leviticus 1:4. The same verb for taking hold of a hand in verse 6 is chazaq, to be strong or to grip, the root of the name Hezekiah and the verb that describes a hand grasping a hand, Isaiah 41:13. God's grip is the reason the Servant cannot fail.

The word 'law' in verse 4 is torah, which means instruction and not only legislation, and 'His law' is something the coastlands wait for. Verse 21 uses the same word again: the LORD was pleased to magnify His torah and make it glorious, so the chapter begins and ends with God's instruction at the centre, first awaited by the nations and then ignored by Israel.

The phrase 'a covenant for the people,' verse 6, is berit am, and the Servant does not merely make a covenant; He is one. 'Light to the nations' joins this to Israel's calling at Sinai to be a kingdom of priests, Exodus 19:5-6. The word for 'blind' is iver and the word for 'deaf' is cheresh, and the pairing is a deliberate undoing of the creation of ears and eyes in Exodus 4:11.

Verse 19 gives a hard word: 'My covenant partner,' meshullam. The root is from shalam, to be complete or to repay, and translators differ over whether it means one who is at peace, one who is rewarded, or one who is fully devoted. The sense is probably the nation in covenant relationship, but the exact shade is uncertain.

The Septuagint of verse 1 reads 'Jacob My servant, I will lay hold of him; Israel My chosen,' so the translators identified the Servant with the nation, and Matthew's quotation drops the names, restoring a personal sense.

typology.type: The bruised reed and the smoldering wick, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: These are not objects but people at the edge of failing: those near to breaking and those nearly out of light. Matthew places the quotation straight after a scene where Jesus withdraws from the Pharisees' plot and heals every one in the crowd, Matthew 12:14-16. The correspondence is the pattern of His ministry, drawing near to the leper, the grieving widow, the tax collector, and the woman caught in sin. The escalation is that He does more than refrain from breaking the weak: He takes the break on Himself, for the one who will not 'grow weak' in verse 4 is crushed in Isaiah 53:5 and 53:10. The type reaches a limit only in that a reed is never repaired by not being broken; Christ must also mend.

Israel's covenants were instruments that God gave through a mediator. Here the Servant is Himself the covenant, and the language reaches its fullest meaning at the Last Supper, where Jesus calls the cup 'the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20. He is not one more messenger of an agreement, since the whole agreement lies in His person: His obedience, death and life. Paul can say that all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Him, 2 Corinthians 1:20. The type is not outrun by its fulfillment; it is simply completed, since no earlier covenant mediator was himself the covenant.

typology.type: Opening the eyes of the blind, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The healing of blind eyes in the Gospels is not an incidental miracle but a sign of the Servant's mission, which is why Jesus answers John the Baptist's doubts by pointing to the blind who receive sight, Matthew 11:4-5. John 9 makes the link explicit: the man born blind is healed, and the leaders who say 'we see' are told their guilt remains, John 9:39-41. That is the same dividing line as verses 18 to 20 of this chapter. The limit of the type is that physical sight is only a sign; the greater blindness, to the Servant Himself, is cured only when the Spirit works in a heart, 2 Corinthians 4:4-6.

Israel as an unseeing servant is a negative type, a picture of what the true Servant is not. The nation had eyes and ears, and the law lay open before it, yet it did not watch or hear. Jesus applies the same pattern to His hearers when He quotes Isaiah 6:9-10, Matthew 13:13-15, and Paul sees it again in the hard hearts of his own people, Romans 11:7-8. In Christ the pattern is reversed, for He is the Servant who hears morning by morning, Isaiah 50:4-5, and who sees what the Father is doing, John 5:19. The limit is that the church is not exempt: the letter to Laodicea describes a people who say they see and are blind, Revelation 3:17.

study.christ:
The most direct link is Matthew 12:15-21, where the evangelist quotes verses 1 to 4 at length. The setting is deliberate. The Pharisees have just plotted to destroy Jesus, Matthew 12:14, and He withdraws rather than fight back, heals the crowds, and warns them not to make Him known. Matthew reads that quiet retreat as the fulfilment of 'He will not quarrel or cry out.' A Messiah who walks away from a confrontation looks weak by human reckoning, but Matthew sees in it the Servant who does not break a bruised reed. The quotation ends with 'In His name the nations will put their hope,' which the Septuagint reading supplies and which tells Matthew's Jewish readers that this Servant's name will be carried beyond Israel, as the Gospel itself ends, Matthew 28:19.

The Spirit-anointing of verse 1 meets Jesus at the Jordan, where the Spirit descends and the voice declares delight in the Son, Matthew 3:16-17. Jesus then reads the next Servant's words from Isaiah 61:1 in the synagogue at Nazareth and says they are fulfilled that day, Luke 4:18-21, and those words speak of liberty for captives and sight for the blind, the very tasks of verse 7. When the imprisoned John asks whether Jesus is the one, He answers by listing the signs this chapter announces, Matthew 11:2-5.

Simeon names the child a 'light for revelation to the Gentiles,' Luke 2:32, and Jesus says of Himself, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12. The risen Lord sends Paul to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light, Acts 26:18, and Paul and Barnabas tell their Gentile hearers that the commission of verse 6 now rests on them as well, Acts 13:47. The church is carrying the Servant's light because the Servant has sent them.

The deepest link is the pairing in the chapter itself: the one who does not break the bruised becomes the one who is bruised. The bruising language returns in the fourth song, where He is 'crushed' for our iniquities, Isaiah 53:5. It is the Servant's gentleness that brings Him to the cross, because He will not defend Himself with force. The prophecy of a justice that He will not abandon, verse 4, runs through that death to its end in the resurrection, Isaiah 53:11 and Acts 3:13-15.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The chapter is also about Israel, and Matthew does not claim that every line of Isaiah 42 is a prediction of a single event in Jesus' life. He claims that the pattern, calling, Spirit, gentleness and the hope of the nations, is gathered up in Him. The blind servant of verse 19 is not Jesus, and to read it that way is to misread the song.
study.god:
The chapter opens a window on a God who does not compete with the empires on their own terms. He is the Creator of verse 5, who gives breath to every person on earth, and yet He is also a God who delights in a single human being in verse 1, using the word 'soul' for what is deepest in Him. The one who stretched out the heavens takes a servant by the hand. Greatness and nearness are not set against each other; they are the same God.

God shows a jealousy for His own name that is not vanity. 'I am the LORD; that is My name,' verse 8, is followed at once by a refusal to share glory. That is the foundation of all He does in the chapter: He sends the Servant, rouses Himself, and punishes Israel because His glory and His name are bound up with His people. A God who yielded His praise to an idol would be a God who left the world to the idols, and so His refusal is also a kindness.

He is a God who declares things before they happen, verse 9, which is the argument of the whole Book of Comfort: the idols cannot announce the future, and He can. The former things, probably His earlier prophecies already fulfilled, give the evidence for the new things that He now announces.

The chapter also holds a surprising tension in verse 14. After a long silence the LORD says He will gasp like a woman in labour. The silence is the exile, felt by the exiles as absence, and the metaphor tells them it was restraint and not indifference. A woman in labour cannot hold back; what has been carried so long is about to be born. The warrior of verse 13 and the labouring mother of verse 14 stand in the same breath, and they belong together.

God is honest about His people's sin and does not hide His part in the judgment. Verse 24 asks, 'Who gave Jacob up for spoil?' and answers, 'Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned?' He does not leave the exiles to conclude that their gods were stronger. The disaster was His discipline, and for that reason it can end by His word. Finally, He is the faithful guide: 'I will lead the blind by a way they did not know,' verse 16, and 'I will not forsake them.' The same people charged with blindness in verse 19 are those He promises to lead. For worship, the chapter calls for a song that is loud enough to reach Kedar and the coastlands, and a quiet trust in the One who will not break what is already bruised.

crossReferences.note: The second Servant Song takes the commission of 42:6 and enlarges it. The Servant is told it is too small a thing to restore Israel, for He is also to be a light to the nations. This shows that the work of 42:1 is not finished in a single stroke but unfolds across the book, and that the Servant is both sent to Israel and beyond her.

A later speaker says the Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Him, and He proclaims liberty to captives and freedom to prisoners. It echoes the Spirit of 42:1 and the prisoners of 42:7, and Jesus reads this very passage in the Nazareth synagogue, Luke 4:18-21, so the two Isaiah texts meet in His mission.

Matthew's longest Old Testament citation of the Servant. He quotes verses 1 to 4 right after Jesus' withdrawal from the plotting Pharisees. His version differs from the Hebrew in some words, and it closes with the nations hoping in His name, matching the Septuagint reading of verse 4.

At the Jordan the Spirit comes down on Jesus and a voice declares delight in Him. The vocabulary of Spirit placed on the chosen one, and a soul that delights, is the vocabulary of Isaiah 42:1, so the baptism is heard as the Servant's commissioning.

The shoot from Jesse's stump has the Spirit of the LORD resting on him and judges the needy with righteousness. It places the same Spirit, the same concern for the weak and the same just rule next to Isaiah 42:1-4, and suggests the Servant and the Davidic king are one figure.

The commission to make a people see and hear without understanding is the hard background to 42:18-20. The nation that was told to be ever hearing and never perceiving is now said to be blind and deaf, so the later charge is not a surprise but the outcome of what Isaiah was sent to do.

The third Servant Song gives the Servant a disciple's ear that is open every morning, in direct contrast to the open ears that do not hear in 42:20. It shows what true hearing looks like, and also the price that the faithful hearer pays.

The Servant is crushed for our iniquities. The crushing here echoes the bruised reed He refused to break in 42:3, though the Hebrew words differ, and so the gentle Servant of chapter 42 and the pierced Servant of chapter 53 are the same person, and the one is the road to the other.

Jesus says He came so that the blind may see and that those who see may become blind. When the Pharisees ask whether they are blind, He says that their claim to sight is the very thing that keeps their guilt. It applies the blind servant of 42:19 to the leaders of His own day.

Paul reports that Jesus sent him to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light. The assignment he received is the commission of 42:7 and 42:16 passed on to the Servant's people, which shows that the Servant's mission continues through those who belong to Him.

Moses warned that a fierce nation from far away would besiege the cities in the land. The fire and battle of 42:25 are the covenant curses that Moses promised if the people did not listen, so the chapter treats the exile as covenant discipline and not an accident of history.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers a question that has been building since Genesis 12. God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his line, and Israel was called at Sinai to be a kingdom of priests, Exodus 19:6. A priestly people stands between God and the nations, and the nations were supposed to see in Israel what God is like. Isaiah 42 recognises that the nation has not done it. Its eyes and ears are shut, and the nations have heard nothing. So the story needs someone who can be, in a single person, what a whole nation failed to be.

That is why the Servant arrives with the Spirit. In Genesis 1:2 the Spirit hovers over the waters before the first light, and here He rests on a person who is to bring light to the nations. Verse 5 begins with the Creator for the same reason: the one commissioning the Servant is the one who made breath, and the work He assigns is a new creation of sight and freedom. The wider story runs through the four songs to the cross and then to the empty tomb, where the Servant's patience is vindicated.

The chapter also sets up the work still to come. The promise of the Servant is not carried out in Isaiah itself; the book ends with a new heavens and a new earth, Isaiah 65:17, and the Servant's people inherit it. The task of verse 6 passes to the church, which carries the gospel to the coastlands, Acts 13:47, and the song of verse 10 begins to be sung from the ends of the earth, as John hears in Revelation 5:9 and 7:9, where a multitude from every nation stands before the throne.

The story ends where the chapter points. The blind are led by a way they did not know, the prisoners are brought out, and darkness gives way to light. In the new Jerusalem the nations walk by the light of God's glory, and the Lamb is its lamp, Revelation 21:23-24. The covenant partner who could not see has been given eyes, and the Servant who did not break the bruised reed has made a people who will not be broken again.

sermon.title: A Bruised Reed He Will Not Break
sermon.why: Keller preaches directly through Isaiah 42:1-9, the first Servant Song at the heart of this chapter, showing how Isaiah's mysterious Servant, depicted as a servant king, a healing king, and a suffering king, is identified in the New Testament as Jesus Christ.

quiz.q: What kind of justice-bringer does the Servant Song describe in verses 1 to 4?

options.text: A gentle Servant who will not break a bruised reed or extinguish a smoldering wick, yet will faithfully establish justice.
options.note: Verses 2 to 4 describe exactly this combination of gentleness and unshakeable faithfulness.

options.text: A loud, forceful ruler who crushes all opposition immediately.
options.note: The opposite; the Servant specifically will not cry out or raise His voice in the streets.

options.text: A distant figure uninterested in the weak or broken.
options.note: The Servant's defining trait is tender care for the bruised and faltering, not indifference.

options.text: A political leader focused solely on military conquest.
options.note: The Servant's mission is described as bringing justice, not military conquest, and through gentleness rather than force.

quiz.q: What mission is given to the Servant in verses 6 to 7?

options.text: To be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners.
options.note: Verses 6 to 7 state this mission directly.

options.text: To conquer foreign nations through military force.
options.note: The opposite; the mission described is covenant, light, healing, and liberation, not conquest.

options.text: To build a new temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: Not the mission described here, which focuses on covenant, light, and liberation rather than construction.

options.text: To rule only over Israel, with no concern for other nations.
options.note: The opposite; the mission explicitly extends to being 'a light to the nations,' beyond Israel alone.

quiz.q: How does Matthew's Gospel use this Servant Song?

options.text: It quotes Isaiah 42:1-4 in full and applies it directly to Jesus' quiet, healing ministry.
options.note: Matthew 12:15-21 does exactly this, one of the clearest direct citations of Isaiah in the New Testament.

options.text: It rejects this passage as irrelevant to Jesus' mission.
options.note: The opposite; Matthew treats this passage as a direct prophecy fulfilled in Jesus.

options.text: It applies the passage only to a future, unnamed prophet.
options.note: Matthew applies it specifically and directly to Jesus, not to an unnamed future figure.

options.text: It uses the passage only as background for Old Testament history with no New Testament application.
options.note: Matthew's quotation is a direct application to Jesus' present ministry, not a mere historical reference.

quiz.q: What painful contrast does verse 19 draw?

options.text: Israel, God's own servant and messenger, is itself blind and deaf.
options.note: Verse 19 asks directly, 'Who is blind but My servant,' exposing Israel's own failure.

options.text: Israel alone among all nations has perfect spiritual sight.
options.note: The opposite; the verse exposes Israel's blindness, not its superior perception.

options.text: Only Israel's enemies are blind, while Israel sees clearly.
options.note: The blindness described is Israel's own, not that of its enemies.

options.text: All nations except Israel struggle with spiritual blindness.
options.note: The specific and pointed accusation in this verse is against Israel, God's own servant, not other nations.

quiz.q: What explanation does the chapter give for Israel being plundered, verses 24 to 25?

options.text: They were unwilling to walk in the LORD's ways and would not obey His law.
options.note: Verse 24 states this reason directly, tying the plunder to Israel's own disobedience.

options.text: They were plundered entirely without cause or reason.
options.note: The opposite; the passage explicitly attributes the plunder to their sin and disobedience.

options.text: Foreign armies were simply stronger with no spiritual cause involved.
options.note: The passage frames the plunder as the LORD's own act of judgment for disobedience, not mere military inferiority.

options.text: It was solely the fault of their political leaders, not the people themselves.
options.note: The text addresses the people's own unwillingness to walk in the LORD's ways, not merely the failure of leadership.

questions: The Servant will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick. Where in your life have you felt like a bruised reed, and how does it change things to know Christ handles you this gently?
The Servant brings justice not through noise and force but through patient faithfulness. Where are you tempted to force a result through pressure rather than trusting God's patient timing?
Israel, God's own servant, is confronted honestly with its blindness and deafness despite having eyes and ears. What is God trying to show you right now that you may be avoiding seeing clearly?
The Servant is called a light to the nations. How are you currently living out that same calling, in Christ, to reflect His light to people around you who do not yet know Him?

The chapter is honest that Israel's suffering came from its own disobedience, not random chance. Is there an area where you need to take responsibility for your own choices rather than blaming your circumstances?

translationNotes.note: This is the first of Isaiah's four Servant Songs, quoted in full in Matthew 12:15-21 and applied directly to Jesus' ministry.
The sharp question 'Who is blind but My servant' uses Israel's own covenant title against itself, exposing the gap between the nation's calling and its actual spiritual condition.
Covenant for the people and light to the nations together describe a mission both to Israel and beyond it, language later applied to Jesus in Luke 2:32 and to the apostolic mission in Acts 13:47.
